blocks.text: Tools let a model act, resources let it read, prompts are the third piece, ready-made instruction templates that a user or client can pick, fill in with specific details, and turn into an actual message sent to the model. This lesson goes deep on prompts, the least talked about of the three, but genuinely useful for making common requests consistent and reusable.
1. What a Prompt Actually Is

blocks.alt: A prompt template gets filled with arguments to become a message

blocks.text: An MCP prompt is a named, reusable instruction template a server offers, something like "summarize this document" or "draft a bug report," rather than the user or a developer typing that same instruction out from scratch every single time, they pick the template and just fill in the specific details.

blocks.title: A useful mental model
blocks.content: A prompt is a lot like a form letter template, the structure and intent stay the same, only the specific filled-in details change each time it is used.

blocks.text: This concept exists specifically because so many requests to an AI model are actually the same handful of common intentions, phrased slightly differently every time, prompts capture and standardize that common intention.
Recognizing which of a user’s common requests are worth turning into a shared prompt template is itself a useful design exercise when building a new server.
2. Anatomy of a Prompt

blocks.alt: A name, description, and arguments make up a prompt

blocks.text: A prompt has a name, a description explaining what it does, and a set of arguments it accepts, similar in spirit to a tool’s inputSchema but describing what the template needs to be filled in correctly.
The arguments list for a prompt mirrors, in spirit, the properties of a tool inputSchema, describing what values are needed and which of them are required before the template can be filled in.

code.content:
# an argument with a default-like optional flag
{"name": "sentence_count", "description": "How many sentences the summary should have", "required": false}

blocks.text: An SDK-based server implementation usually lets an author define a prompt using a simple decorated function, similar to how tools are registered, rather than assembling this JSON shape by hand.
3. Discovering Prompts: prompts/list
Just like tools and resources, prompts are discovered rather than hardcoded, a client calls prompts/list to see what templates a server currently offers.
Like tools and resources, a client typically caches this list for the duration of a session rather than re-fetching it before every single use.
Some clients render this discovered list directly as clickable suggestions in a chat interface, turning prompt discovery into a genuinely visible part of the end user experience.
4. Using a Prompt: prompts/get

blocks.alt: A client sends prompts/get to receive a filled prompt

blocks.text: Once a client knows which prompt it wants, and has the values to fill in its arguments, it calls prompts/get, the server returns the fully filled-in message, ready to send to the model.

The result of prompts/get is typically a list of one or more ready-to-send messages, already filled in with the specific argument values supplied, requiring no further template processing by the client.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Method","Purpose"],"rows":[["prompts/list","Discover available templates"],["prompts/get","Fill in a specific template with real values"]]}

blocks.text: If a required argument is missing when prompts/get is called, the server should reject the request clearly, the same way a tool call rejects a missing required parameter.
5. Prompts vs Tools vs Resources

blocks.alt: A prompt is a template, a tool is an action, and a resource is data

blocks.text: It helps to see all three side by side, since a new server author often has to decide which bucket a new piece of functionality belongs in.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Concept","What it is","How it is used"],"rows":[["Tool","An action","Invoked with tools/call"],["Resource","Readable content","Fetched with resources/read"],["Prompt","An instruction template","Filled in with prompts/get"]]}

blocks.text: A quick test that helps distinguish all three, does it act (tool), does it provide raw content (resource), or does it produce a ready-made instruction (prompt).

blocks.title: A one-line summary
blocks.content: Tools do, resources inform, prompts instruct, all three ultimately feed into what the model sees and can act on.

code.content:
# calling each of the three, side by side
client.call_tool("send_email", {...})
client.read_resource("file:///report.txt")
client.get_prompt("summarize_document", {...})

blocks.text: 6. Why Reusable Prompts Are Useful

Without a shared prompt, every application that wants to offer "summarize this document" as an option has to write its own version of that instruction, often slightly differently worded each time, a shared MCP prompt means the exact same well-tested instruction is available consistently everywhere it is needed.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Without shared prompts","With MCP prompts"],"rows":[["Each app writes its own instruction wording","One well-tested template reused everywhere"],["Improving the wording means updating every app","Improving the wording updates it everywhere at once"]]}

blocks.text: This consistency benefit compounds the same way it does for tools and resources, the more applications that reuse the same well-crafted prompt, the more collective value that one piece of careful wording provides.

This is especially valuable for anything involving careful, precise wording, a legal disclaimer prompt or a safety-sensitive instruction benefits enormously from being written once, reviewed carefully, and reused everywhere unchanged.
7. Arguments Make a Prompt Flexible

blocks.alt: A prompt template takes an argument to produce a customized prompt

blocks.text: A prompt without arguments could only ever say exactly the same fixed thing, arguments let one template serve many specific situations, "summarize this specific document in this specific number of sentences" rather than a single hardcoded example.

code.content:
# same template, different arguments, different outcomes
client.get_prompt("summarize_document", {"document_text": doc_a, "sentence_count": "2"})
client.get_prompt("summarize_document", {"document_text": doc_b, "sentence_count": "5"})

blocks.text: Required arguments should be kept to the genuine minimum a template needs to function, every additional required argument is one more thing a caller has to supply correctly before the prompt can even be used.
An optional argument with a sensible fallback behavior, like defaulting sentence_count to three when not supplied, keeps a template easy to use while still allowing more control when needed.
8. Prompts Can Pull in Resources

blocks.alt: A prompt pulls in a resource

blocks.text: A prompt template can be designed to automatically pull in a resource’s content as part of filling itself in, for instance a "review this file" prompt might take a file URI as an argument and internally read that resource to build its final message, this connection is covered in depth in the Context Injection lesson in the MCP Prompts module.

This connection between prompts and resources is one of the more powerful patterns in MCP, letting a single prompt argument, like a file URI, expand into an entire piece of live, current content automatically.

code.content:
# a prompt handler internally reading a resource
def review_file_prompt(file_uri):
    content = read_resource(file_uri)
    return [{"role": "user", "content": f"Please review this file:\n{content}"}]

blocks.text: This is a genuinely elegant piece of composition, a single prompt argument can quietly expand into a full document worth of context, without the caller needing to manually fetch and paste that content in themselves.
9. Prompts Are Often User-Facing

Unlike tools, which a model typically decides to call on its own, prompts are frequently surfaced directly to a human user, as a menu of suggested actions, "summarize," "translate," "draft a reply," letting the user pick one deliberately rather than relying on the model to infer what they want.

blocks.title: A practical implication
blocks.content: Because a human might see a prompt name and description directly, they deserve the same care in wording as any other piece of user-facing text, clear, friendly, and specific.

blocks.text: Some host applications render the prompt list as a literal slash-command style menu, letting a user type a short trigger to select and fill in a specific template quickly.

blocks.title: A design implication
blocks.content: Because a user might pick a prompt by name alone before seeing its full description, a clear, memorable name matters even more here than it does for a tool a model selects programmatically.

blocks.text: 10. Designing a Good Prompt Template

A good prompt template is specific enough to produce a consistently useful result, but general enough to be reused across many different inputs, striking this balance is the main design skill involved in building a useful prompt library for a server.
A useful test while designing a template is imagining ten different real situations it might be used for, if the template only really fits one of them well, it is probably too narrow.

blocks.title: A helpful exercise
blocks.content: Write the template wording first without any variables filled in, then check whether it still reads naturally once you mentally substitute a few very different example values.

blocks.text: Naming a prompt clearly, the same way a tool needs a clear name, also matters, summarize_document communicates intent far better than a vague name like doc_helper.
11. Prompt Versioning in Brief

A prompt template can change over time, its wording refined, an argument added, this is covered fully in the Prompt Versioning lesson in the MCP Prompts module, for now it is worth knowing a prompt is not necessarily a permanently fixed piece of text.

A small wording change to an existing template is usually harmless, but changing what arguments a template requires can break any existing caller relying on the old shape, exactly the kind of change protocol versioning and capability negotiation help manage.
Treat a published prompt template with the same care you would treat a public function signature, changing what it requires can quietly break every caller depending on the old version.
12. Prompts Across Different Host Applications

Because prompts are discovered through the same standard MCP mechanism as tools and resources, the exact same prompt template can appear consistently across many different host applications, a chat app and a code editor can both offer the identical "summarize this document" prompt, sourced from the same server.
This consistency is exactly the same reuse benefit tools and resources provide, extended to the specific case of common, reusable instructions.

blocks.text: 13. A Worked Example
Trace using a translation prompt template, filling it with a specific piece of text and a target language.

code.content:
filled = client.get_prompt("translate_text", {"text": "Good morning", "target_language": "Spanish"})
print(filled["messages"])   # a ready-to-send message asking the model to translate

blocks.text: Notice the model never needed a hardcoded, hand-written translation instruction, the prompt template supplied a consistent, already-tested wording, only the specific text and language varied.

code.content:
# the same template reused for a different language pair
filled2 = client.get_prompt("translate_text", {"text": "Thank you", "target_language": "French"})

blocks.text: This same pattern, one template, many concrete uses, is exactly what makes prompts worth building in the first place, rather than just writing a one-off instruction by hand each time.
14. Common Mistakes When Working With Prompts

items: Confusing a prompt with a tool, and expecting it to perform an action rather than simply producing a filled-in message.
Designing a prompt template so specific it only works for one exact input, defeating the purpose of reusability.
Forgetting to validate prompt arguments, allowing a malformed or malicious value to end up inside the final message unexamined.
Assuming prompts are only for internal use, when they are often meant to be shown directly to an end user as a menu of options.

blocks.text: A fifth common mistake is putting sensitive or untrusted data directly into a prompt argument without any sanitization, a concern covered fully in the Prompt Security lesson in the MCP Prompts module.
A sixth common mistake is exposing a prompt with no clear description, leaving both a human user and a client library guessing at what selecting it will actually produce.
A seventh common mistake is not testing a prompt template with a genuinely unusual or edge-case input, only with the one clean example used while designing it.
15. Practice: Design a Prompt Library
Sketch three prompt templates a customer support MCP server might offer, drafting a reply, escalating a ticket, and summarizing a conversation, including the arguments each one would need.
Once you have sketched these three, consider which one might benefit from pulling in a resource automatically, such as escalate_ticket reading the original ticket record as part of filling itself in.

blocks.title: One more thing to try
blocks.content: Try writing out the exact filled-in message your escalate_ticket prompt would produce for a specific, concrete ticket, to see whether the wording still reads naturally.

blocks.text: Key Takeaway

A prompt is a reusable instruction template, discovered with prompts/list and filled in with prompts/get, distinct from tools, which act, and resources, which are read, prompts often surface directly to end users as a menu of consistent, well-tested requests.

This lesson closes the brief tour of what a server can expose, tools, resources, and prompts, having now covered each in real depth. The next lesson, Context, steps back to look at how all of this, tools, resources, and prompts together, actually feeds into what a model sees at any given moment.

The prompt-resource connection from the newly added section is worth remembering as you move into the Context lesson next, since it is one of the clearest examples of how tools, resources, and prompts work together rather than in isolation.
